articles.title: Updated NBA Power Rankings After Kuminga, Watson, DeRozan, Klay Deals
articles.summary: It's been a wild offseason for the NBA. And as it heads to September, the moves are still rolling in.
articles.body:
It's been a wild offseason for the NBA. And as it heads to September, the moves are still rolling in.

Since we last checked in (on the heels of LeBron James choosing the Philadelphia 76ers), we've seen Peyton Watson go to the Cleveland Cavaliers, DeMar DeRozan join the Denver Nuggets and Jonathan Kuminga sign with the Minnesota Timberwolves.

Now, we're here to once again sort through the entire league in the form of power rankings.

We'll use the same criteria that's guided us for years (team and player stats, recent performance, championship chances and plenty of subjectivity), but an offseason edition naturally requires more projection than usual.

Below, you'll find how the entire league stacks up nearly a week into free agency.

ATL | BKN | BOS | CHA | CHI | CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GSW | HOU | IND | LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN | NOP | NYK | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX | POR | SAC | SAS | TOR | UTA | WAS

Russell Westbrook retired, and DeMar DeRozan took a buyout, but those changes felt inevitable, and the Sacramento Kings didn't chase any veterans to replace them.

That left first-round picks Darius Acuff and Alex Karaban as their most meaningful additions. And the approach that led to that result was the right one to take.

Acuff, especially, should get tons of developmental minutes this coming season, since the Kings should really have nothing to prioritize over him and the possibility that this could soon be his team.

After finally trading Giannis Antetokounmpo, the Milwaukee Bucks seem like a near-shoo-in for the 2027 lottery.

Yes, Tyler Herro, Jaime Jaquez Jr. and Kel'el Ware could make them a bit more competitive than expected in the short term, but with fewer teams openly tanking, it's hard to see this roster outperforming many others in the East.

So this season (and maybe the next couple after it), will be as much about the development of incoming rookies Brayden Burries and Nate Ament and new coach Taylor Jenkins as it is about anything else.

The Brooklyn Nets drafted Mikel Brown with the No. 6 pick in this summer's draft. And there will certainly be plenty of time and attention paid to his development.

But the rest of the offseason suggests Brooklyn wants to be more competitive than the 20-62 team it was in 2025-26.

Adding Julius Randle (who was essentially salary-dumped to them), Keon Ellis and Mo Wagner are all win-now moves. Re-signing Day'Ron Sharpe, who looks ready to start in place of the recently traded Nicolas Claxton, is too.

If Michael Porter Jr. can stay healthy and some of the young incumbents (like Egor Dëmin) show some real improvement, the Nets could win more games than they did last season.

But they still feel like a safe bet to be in the mix for the East's worst record.

Offseason Overreactions for Every Team 🫨

The Chicago Bulls lost some firepower with Collin Sexton going to the Los Angeles Lakers and Anfernee Simons signing with the Philadelphia 76ers, but they still have a real shot to be better in 2026-27.

Hopefully, Josh Giddey can give them more than 54 games this season, because he has a pair of dynamic finishers joining him in Nicolas Claxton and rookie Caleb Wilson.

And the losses of Sexton and Simons certainly hurt a lot less when news of Norman Powell joining the team broke.

Chicago is still likely to lose more games than it wins, but there's now a solid mix of veteran (Giddey, Claxton and Powell) and young (Wilson and Matas Buzelis) talent.

The Memphis Grizzlies finally found a trade partner for Ja Morant (who's now on the Portland Trail Blazers), and they've officially entered a new era.

It'll be led by Cameron Boozer, but there's plenty of other young (or at least young-ish) talent in place with Cedric Coward, Zach Edey and Cam Spencer.

The Grizzlies will lose a lot of games based on little more than the experience gap, but they're talented, competitive and will be a tougher out than opponents realize.

Since the New Orleans Pelicans traded their 2026 first-round pick last summer for Derik Queen, they don't really have any incoming rookies to be excited about.

And for most of free agency, their only move was re-signing soon-to-be-38-year-old DeAndre Jordan.

Pelicans fans might have some hope improvement from Queen and a bit more availability from Zion Williamson, Trey Murphy and Dejounte Murray, but the likelier outcome is another season without a playoff appearance.

And though they recently added Bennedict Mathurin on a low-cost, two-year deal, his shoot-first game might not mesh with all the ball-dominant players already there. If he does play well, it feels like a near-guarantee that he'd decline his player option for the second season.

Ultimately, it just feels like New Orleans sort of tread water this season.

There are still some veterans in place (like Darius Garland and Brandon Ingram) who'll occasionally make the Los Angeles Clippers competitive, but the Kawhi Leonard trade was obviously a pretty big pivot toward the future.

This roster is now about young prospects like Keaton Wagler and Yanic Konan Niederhäuser.

Garland and Ingram might even become trade candidates between now and February, as L.A. likely wants to end up in the lottery to add even more talent to the new foundation.

The Utah Jazz lost restricted free agent Walker Kessler to the Los Angeles Lakers, but they got two future first-round picks and two first-round pick swaps out of the sign-and-trade.

There was no way they could pass up that kind of value, especially since there's likely enough talent in place to start being competitive without him.

If everyone's healthy, a rotation with Keyonte George, rookie Darryn Peterson, Ace Bailey, Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr. is going to be dynamic offensively and awfully long on the other end.

If one or two of Cody Williams, Kyle Filipowski or Isaiah Collier takes a big developmental step, this team might even contend for a play-in spot.

By replacing Grayson Allen and Royce O'Neale with Miles Bridges and Luke Kennard, the Phoenix Suns probably have a little more raw talent, but those departing wings were a big part of the gritty mentality that made Phoenix one of last season's biggest surprises.

And it remains to be seen whether Kennard and Bridges can buy into the defense- and team-first mentality that made the Suns what they were last season.

If they do, Devin Booker will have a bit better offensive talent to play off of. And even if other teams in the West improve, Phoenix could finish in the mid-40s again.

The Golden State Warriors were on the short list of teams LeBron James thought about joining. And had he wound up there, the story would've been plenty of fun.

Stephen Curry and LeBron James met in the Finals four times. They were the NBA's biggest rivalry of the 2010s. They had a magical run as teammates in the 2024 Olympics. Ending their careers together would make for a nice bow on this era.

But at their ages, and despite how well the best versions of their games mesh, it was always hard to see that possibility as much more than a great story.

The top-tier Western Conference contenders (like the San Antonio Spurs, Oklahoma City Thunder and maybe even Minnesota Timberwolves) will simply be too fast, too athletic and too hungry for the Warriors (with or without LeBron) to seriously contend for a title.

And that's still true after the recent additions of Brandon Williams and Georges Niang, though both could be genuinely helpful role players.

The Washington Wizards will undoubtedly be better than they were last season.

The rotation now includes Anthony Davis, the recently re-signed Trae Young and incoming first overall pick AJ Dybantsa. Just adding that trio to the existing rotation could double Washington's 2025-26 win total.

But they also got deeper in the frontcourt by trading Jaden Hardy and two second-round picks for Deandre Ayton. And if one or two of the incumbents (like Alex Sarr, Tre Johnson, Bilal Coulibaly or Kyshawn George) show serious development, the playoffs aren't out of the question.

The Dallas Mavericks adding Santi Aldama, Zaccharie Risacher and even Tarik Biberović to a squad with Kyrie Irving returning from injury, Cooper Flagg coming off a Rookie of the Year campaign and Dusty May making the jump from college coaching to the NBA makes them pretty interesting.

They still feel like a long shot to make the playoffs, but the play-in wouldn't be a shocking place to end up.

If one of their incoming first-round picks (Morez Johnson or Sergio de Larrea) is ready to help right away, that might even be the floor.

With the price only being Jerami Grant and Kris Murray, the Portland Trail Blazers really couldn't afford not to trade for Ja Morant.

Sure, he comes with some baggage, particularly the injury history, but he's also an immense talent with a little over three years till his 30th birthday.

And Portland, with the defense of Toumani Camara, Deni Avdija and Donovan Clingan, has a great roster to cover Ja's weaknesses.

There will be a bit of a learning curve as he and Damian Lillard figure out how to play together. It may take both guards some time to accept that Avdija is now the face of the team.

But after the Blazers sort through all of that, they should be in the hunt for another playoff appearance.

After closing the 2025-26 campaign as perhaps the NBA's hottest team, the Charlotte Hornets unloaded two of their top four scorers in LaMelo Ball and Miles Bridges and didn't replace them with any real starpower in the short term.

But they did add draft capital in those moves and re-signed Coby White. And Grayson Allen, Dorian Finney-Smith, Royce O'Neale and Naz Reid all have plenty of experience supporting star wings.

That's exactly what Charlotte is betting Brandon Miller and Kon Knueppel will become. And last season gave the Hornets plenty of evidence for it.

The Indiana Pacers losing their 2026 first-round pick was a massive blow. Getting Ivica Zubac out of the gap year was good, but him and a top-four pick obviously would've been better.

They weren't really able to erase the sting of that loss with free-agency acquisitions either, though Kelly Oubre Jr. could certainly help the rotation.

Ultimately, Indiana fans have to hope that the return of Tyrese Haliburton and better health from the rest of the rotation will get the team back to the level it hit in its run to the 2025 Finals.

The Orlando Magic had a pretty quiet offseason that included re-signing Jevon Carter and Jonathan Isaac (after they released him from his prior contract) and replacing the outgoing Mo Wagner with old friend Nikola Vučević.

That last move could probably be viewed as a raw talent upgrade, but Vuč is now well past his prime, and his value is heavily dependent on whether he’s hitting threes on a given night.

What this summer is more likely about is the front office’s faith in the Paolo Banchero-Franz Wagner pairing and its hope that new coach Sean Sweeney can draw more out of the team than Jamahl Mosley did.

It’s not a crazy bet. There’s a lot of talent on the roster. It’s been derailed by injuries in back-to-back seasons now. And when it got relatively healthy ahead of the first round, Orlando nearly eliminated the Detroit Pistons in the 1-8 matchup.

By the end of the postseason, the Atlanta Hawks had as many playoff wins (two) against the New York Knicks as the rest of the NBA (one).

And they followed that up with what appears to be a purely additive offseason.

CJ McCollum and Jock Landale were both re-signed. Rookie Kingston Flemings brings some upside to the backcourt. And though Jonathan Kuminga is out, Atlanta added Aaron Wiggins and Devin Carter in a pair of salary dumps from other teams. Wiggins, specifically, is absolutely capable of replacing Kuminga's production.

That and continued development from Jalen Johnson, Dyson Daniels and Onyeka Okongwu could have Atlanta pushing for 50 wins next season.

The Los Angeles Lakers' LeBron James era is over, and their first moves in the wake of it were re-signing Luka Dončić's secondary playmaker and adding a rim-running, rim-protecting center.

Those were two key ingredients in the Dallas Mavericks' run to the 2024 NBA Finals. And while Austin Reaves may not quite reach Kyrie Irving's level and Walker Kessler has struggled with durability, you can at least understand L.A.'s philosophy.

Collin Sexton, Quentin Grimes and Sandro Mamukelashvili don't really check the three-and-D boxes quite as cleanly as some of Luka's other teammates in Dallas, but all three can at least shoot.

Offensively, L.A. should be about as explosive as anyone in the league. The other end depends an awful lot on whether Kessler lives up to his new four-year, $130 million deal.

The Toronto Raptors may have made the biggest offseason leap of anyone when they traded Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, two future first-round picks, two second-round picks and a first-round pick swap for Kawhi Leonard.

Even with seven years between now and the last time Toronto traded for him, the move feels eerily similar to when the Raptors acquired Leonard for a package built around DeMar DeRozan.

He's once again a massive upgrade over the key player going out, and the young core still in place might be even better than it was in 2019. Leonard, Scottie Barnes and Collin Murray-Boyles could be the foundation of a terrifying defense.

And Kawhi now gives this team one of the game's best individual closers. Or at least he could give them that. Shortly after the deal was reported, we learned that the teams were putting it on hold pending the results of the NBA's investigation into possible salary cap circumvention involving Kawhi and the Los Angeles Clippers.

Right now, we'll operate under the assumption that the deal ultimately goes through in some form or another. If it doesn't, we'll obviously have to adjust our outlook on Toronto.

The Houston Rockets quietly got better and more experienced this offseason, adding Bogdan Bogdanović and Marcus Smart before re-signing Tari Eason.

Reed Sheppard and Amen Thompson should still have inside tracks on minutes in the backcourt, but Bogdanović can provide some tutelage for both on the offensive end, while Smart provides it on defense.

With that rotation shored up, Fred VanVleet rejoining it and Kevin Durant and Alperen Şengün coming back to the frontcourt, Houston could be closer to contention next season.

There are very real questions about the offensive fit between Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo. The lack of three-point shooting from both could make the court feel pretty cramped on that end.

But they'll do the same thing to opponents on the other end of the floor, too. With those two, Davion Mitchell and Andrew Wiggins in the rotation, Miami has a chance to have a top-five defense.

And following the additions of Tim Hardaway Jr. and Klay Thompson, some of the concerns about the entire team's shooting may already be vanquished. With those two, Wiggins and Mitchell, there should be enough room for Giannis to dominate slashing lanes.

If everything clicks, the best version of this team can win the title.

There was some rumbling earlier in the offseason about restricted free agent Jalen Duren wanting to move on from the Detroit Pistons.

And while he remains unsigned, " spending power " around the NBA has dried up to the point that no one can really sign him to the kind of offer sheet that would make Detroit balk at matching it.

The likeliest outcome is that the Pistons will run it back with Duren, Cade Cunningham and most of the rest of the scrappy supporting cast that helped Detroit finish first in the East.

In that case, the only thing that could really cause another team leap would be a star turn from Ausar Thompson, which certainly isn't out of the question.

The Cleveland Cavaliers were among the teams chasing LeBron James. And though they missed out on him, they got about as good a consolation as they could later in the offseason.

Thanks to a sign-and-trade that cost them Max Strus and future picks (one first and one second), the Cavs added Peyton Watson's versatile defense, above-the-rim finishing and burgeoning catch-and-shoot skills.

Shortly after pulling off that move, they re-signed James Harden and gave themselves one of the best and most complete starting fives in the NBA.

Harden, Donovan Mitchell, Watson, Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen bring plenty of playmaking, defense and shooting. And Cleveland is a real contender to represent the East in the Finals.

Losing Watson obviously hurts in the long term, but DeMar DeRozan instantly joined the Sixth Man of the Year mix when he signed with the Denver Nuggets.

He's a better scorer than Watson right now, and his isolation abilities will boost a second-unit offense that has struggled for seriousness for years.

If DeRozan and Marvin Bagley (one of this summer's more underrated additions) can help Denver even be neutral in the non-Nikola Jokić minutes, one of the best starting fives in the NBA should get this team to 50-plus wins again.

It's fair to wonder how the usage will be split between four ball-dominant stars (Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey, LeBron and Jaylen Brown) and a rising potential star (VJ Edgecombe). LeBron's age and Embiid's health are major concerns too.

But in terms of pure talent, it's hard to find many rosters in the entire NBA that can go toe to toe with this one.

When healthy, Embiid is still one of the most dominant scorers in the NBA. Maxey is one of its best and most dynamic playmakers. LeBron is still a top 30-40 player. And Brown, who just spent the last few years proving he's one of the best second options in the league, will instantly be its best fourth option.

Add a bench headlined by Anfernee Simons and Dean Wade, and it's easy to see this team contending for a title.

There will certainly be an adjustment period for Anthony Edwards and LaMelo Ball. Both are used to having the ball in their hands and engineering possessions from scratch. Both will have to get a little more comfortable allowing the other to do that.

But if you sort of combine Minnesota's two big trades (the other being a Julius Randle salary dump), it's hard to see the LaMelo-Randle swap as anything but a big upgrade for the Wolves.

Ball is a defense-bending playmaker who'll create more looks (and more efficient looks) for Edwards than Randle did.

And while it looked for a bit like that move might make the Timberwolves a lot smaller, landing Kuminga keeps them among the biggest and most athletic teams in the NBA.

The Boston Celtics authored the most controversial move of the summer when they traded Jaylen Brown for Paul George, two first-round picks and two second-round picks.

But if you look at the deal pragmatically (as the Celtics did), it's not all that difficult to understand their thinking.

Boston just won 56 games without Tatum for most of the season. He'll be back for 2026-27. The one-to-one swap of Tatum for Brown is an upgrade. Then, George will slide into a role that simply didn't exist for the 2025-26 team (because Tatum was recovering).

George isn't the player he was a few years ago, but he's still a reliable three-point shooter, a much better playmaker than Brown and a more willing complementary piece (Brown plays like a high-volume star).

Add to that the fact that Boston landed Mitchell Robinson and will bring back Derrick White, Payton Pritchard and coach Joe Mazzulla, and it's not all that difficult to still see Boston as a contender.

In today's NBA (which includes the dreaded second apron), sustainable contention is almost impossible with a top 25-35 player like Brown being paid like a top-10 player. Boston realized that and pivoted.

The Oklahoma City Thunder made some predictable cost-cutting moves by trading Isaiah Joe and Aaron Wiggins, and Luguentz Dort might be next.

And while it might fly in the face of conventional wisdom to shed good players from a title contender, it's almost a requirement to survive under the current collective bargaining agreement. OKC has a good track record for developing talent, and there are multiple potential difference-makers on rookie contracts still on the roster.

But ultimately, the Thunder getting back to the mountaintop probably depends on little more than health. It's reasonable to believe that if OKC had Jalen Williams and Ajay Mitchell at 100 percent, it would've beaten the San Antonio Spurs in the Western Conference Finals.

The San Antonio Spurs entered the offseason with few (if any needs). On nothing more than internal development, the team that represented the West in the Finals would've had a shot to win it all in 2026-27.

But they haven't just stood still. San Antonio added veteran forward Tobias Harris to Victor Wembanyama, Dylan Harper and Stephon Castle. He'll provide a boost in experience, shooting and size to the second unit.

And again, the starting five could be better simply by getting a year older (and maybe plugging Harper into one of those spots).

The Spurs' 2025-26 campaign ended in heartbreak, but they have the talent to win it all in 2026-27.

The reigning champions are bringing back their entire starting five. That's the most important takeaway from their offseason. And that alone makes them contenders to repeat.

But bringing back Landry Shamet and Jose Alvarado were big moves too. And though the loss of Mitchell Robinson could sting, replacing him with Andre Drummond makes sense.

New York will probably need one or two unexpected breakouts like the one Shamet had in 2025-26, but they have a very real shot to break the no-repeat-champion curse that has lived with the NBA for nearly a decade.

articles.title: What’s going on with Kyle Singler? 6-foot-8 ex-Thunder star posts disturbing video about Coach K
articles.summary: NBA News: Kyle Singler is at the center of a troubling story after the former Duke standout posted a string of rambling Instagram videos this week, aiming point.
articles.body: Kyle Singler is at the center of a troubling story after the former Duke standout posted a string of rambling Instagram videos this week, aiming pointed accusations at his old college coach, Mike Krzyzewski. The clips show him pacing through what looks like an empty house, insisting people are trying to hurt him and take his money.It's a jarring turn for a guy once known for hitting big shots on college basketball's biggest stage. Now the questions aren't about his jumper. They're about his safety.What's going on with Kyle Singler?The videos surfaced on Tuesday night, and they don't look good. Kyle Singler, 38, wanders from room to room, appears to be agitated, describing a life that sounds nothing like the one he built during his NBA years. He says his power has been shut off. He says his house has been broken into. He says money is being drained from accounts he can barely track anymore.None of that has been independently verified. But the pattern is familiar to anyone who followed his last public flare-up. Back in November 2024, Singler posted something similar, telling followers he feared for his life every single day. This week's videos pick up roughly where that one left off, only louder and more disjointed.There's also history sitting underneath all of this. Singler was arrested in Oklahoma last October after his girlfriend told police he grabbed her by the head and shoved her to the ground during an argument at an Airbnb, with their child present. He posted bond on a misdemeanor charge and the case has largely stayed out of headlines since, until now.What did Kyle Singler say about Coach K?Singler didn't just vent about strangers or unnamed enemies. He went after Krzyzewski directly, the coach who guided him to a national title in 2010 and later called him one of the most complete players he'd ever developed.Singler claims he reached out for help and got nothing back. "Coach K has set me up, man," he said in one clip, adding that Krzyzewski had "fully dismissed" his messages.“You guys are cutting my power off, breaking into my house, stealing money, ruining my life. I reached out to Coach K and all he did was sit me on the bench. Thanks, man. Is that what we're doing at that school, sitting people down, teaching them up? Cool beans, man. Coach, where you at? Help a brother out. Thought we were on the same team, man," Singler shared.He described feeling abandoned by the program he once helped define, at one point comparing his situation to being benched, as though the man who shaped his career had simply stopped answering the phone.It's worth remembering where Singler came from. He was the engine of Duke's 2010 championship run, earned Most Outstanding Player honors in that tournament, and went on to play seven NBA seasons split between Detroit and Oklahoma City after going 33rd overall in 2011. He pulled in more than $22 million over his career, most of it from a contract extension with the Thunder.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: La cantera de España es la envidia de Europa
articles.standfirst: Otro verano mágico con seis medallas, más que ningún otro país del continente. Dos oros y tres bronces en Europeos y una plata Mundial
articles.summary: Ha ganado seis medallas, más que ningún otro país del continente, en los siete campeonatos que ha participado. Dos oros y tres bronces en Europeos y una plata Mundial
articles.body: España lleva ya muchos años siendo la envidia de toda Europa por los éxitos que de forma casi recurrente y mantenida en el tiempo cosechan sus selecciones de formación. Este verano lo ha vuelto a hacer con seis medallas, incluidos dos oros continentales y una plata mundial, en los siete campeonatos en los que que ha contado con representación masculina o femenina. El formidable botín estival de España asciende a dos oros (Eurobasket femeninos Sub 16 y Sub 18), una plata (Mundial femenino Sub 17) y tres bronces (Eurobasket masculino Sub 16 y Sub 20 masculino y femenino). Sólo la Sub 18 masculina (4º puesto) se quedó fuera del podio. Las selecciones de cantera de España han conquistado más medallas que nadie en Europa, superando las cinco de Francia (1+2+2), y las tres de Eslovenia (2+1+0), la única que la iguala en el capítulo de oros con dos. Y el balance de victorias y derrotas de las selecciones españoles en los seis campeonatos en los que tocaron metal fue superlativo: 38-4. Las niñas de la Sub 16 revalidaron título en el Eurobasket de Rumanía tras firmar un torneo perfecto, ganando sus siete partidos por una diferencia media de 68,7 puntos. Arrasaron de principio a fin, aplastando en la primera fase a Bulgaria 13-128, récord del torneo, y a Eslovenia en la final (87-40). Amelia Alonso (MVP) y Paula Reynal fueron incluidas en el quinteto ideal del torneo. Otras que lo bordaron fueron las Sub 17 en el Mundial de la República Checa con una plata que supo a oro asustando en la final a la inaccesible Estados Unidos (82-73). La española Isa Hernández (17+4,7+3,9) integró el cinco ideal del torneo y fue elegida MVP de la final (28+4+4+8 robos). Y la seleccionadora española, Isabel Fernández 'Moses' fue elegida mejor entrenadora del campeonato. La selección femenina Sub 18 se coronó en el Eurobasket de Suecia tras arrollar a Francia en la final (82-46), obteniendo la clasificación para el Mundial Sub 19 de 2027 con Somto Okafor, escolta de 1,76 m, como MVP del torneo. España demostró una superioridad abrumadora de principio a fin, terminando invicta el campeonato (7-0) y ganando sus partidos por una diferencia media de 45,2 puntos. No en vano, fue el séptimo título que conquistan las nuestras en esta categoría. Las selecciones masculina y femenina Sub 20 también subieron al podio en sus respectivos Europeos, en ambos casos para colgarse la medalla de bronce. Las chicas lo hicieron en Lituania tras caer en semifinales ante Francia (54-64) y aplastar a Bélgica por el tercer puesto (81-59). Además, Inés Sotelo fue incluida en el cinco ideal del torneo. Y los chicos lo lograron en el campeonato que tuvo lugar en Eslovenia. Tras un inicio brillante, perdieron en semifinales con Serbia (65-72), pero se rehicieron de la decepción imponiéndose a Francia en la lucha por el tercer puesto (54-65). El base español Raúl Villar, máximo asistente del campeonato con una media de 7 pases por encuentro, formó parte del quinteto ideal del torneo. Por último, los niños españoles de la Sub 16 también subieron al podio en el Eurobasket de Rumanía. Tras un campeonato inmaculado, tropezaron en semifinales en un partido a cara o cruz ante Letonia (87-92), pero se resarcieron en la lucha por el tercer puesto en otro partido igualadísimo ante Lituania (93-96). Rhys Robinson, escolta español de 1,97 m del Real Madrid, fue incluido en el quinteto ideal del torneo. Elisa Aguilar, presidenta de la FEB, celebró otra cosecha triunfal de la cantera española: “Un verano más, nuestras Selecciones han sido sobre la pista el fiel reflejo de lo que queremos ser. Equipos que han competido a la perfección y que han demostrado en todo momento su carácter ganador para poder optar a medalla en la totalidad de los campeonatos". Los éxitos refuerzan a su juicio la apuesta por descubrir y cuidar el talento desde edades muy tempranas: "Seguimos una línea de trabajo que ayuda a nuestros jugadores y jugadoras a seguir creciendo y que aseguran cada verano el relevo generacional de unas Selecciones absolutas que se nutren de todo este trabajo”.

articles.title: Trump’s ambassador to Italy is cruising the Med on a $450M yacht
articles.summary: Tilman Fertitta, a 69-year-old Texan billionaire, has been cruising around Italy all summer on his floating mansion. We come aboard this unconventional diplomacy tour.
articles.body: Tilman Fertitta, the US ambassador to Italy, wants everyone to see he has a very normal kitchen. It’s just a casual setup, a place where a regular person can duck in to eat some cold leftover taco meat out of a plastic tub, as he is doing right now. “I haven’t eaten all day,” he confides. Fertitta points out that it is, in fact, unusual how ordinary the kitchen is, given that it is part of his $450 million yacht, the Boardwalk. The ambassador, a 69-year-old Texan billionaire, insisted on installing it, to have a place for the ship owner’s family to hang out, maybe flip an omelet for themselves. “Big boats never have a family kitchen,” he says. This is near the end of an extensive tour of the enormous, gleaming vessel. We’ve come aboard during one of the last stops on a diplomatic cruise of coastal Italy by the Trump administration’s envoy. The summer voyage, which began in June, has included dockings in Sicily, Venice and Sardinia. Today we’re in one of Italy’s largest seaports, Port Livorno, about 200 miles from Rome. The ambassador and his entourage were late to arrive from a weekend in glitzy Portofino on the Italian Riveria after a violent storm slowed the 380 foot long, six-tier high (seven if you count the small observation deck) yacht’s journey. Fertitta, who ranks 109 on Forbes 400 list of wealthiest Americans, made his fortune in the hospitality and entertainment industry. His summer project with the Boardwalk is all about nurturing diplomatic relations between the US and Italy by playing the role of approachable host on the immaculate floating mansion. In advance of the latest in the series of receptions, whirring Dyson vacuums are gobbling up storm debris and deckhands in matching nautical uniform are putting back the decorations that had been battened down during the storm in what looks like fine-tuned behind-the-scenes choreography. Throughout the afternoon we see chrome railings polished, pillows plumped, red carpets rolled out — all while Fertitta’s loyal second officer, Carter Skains, makes sure our curious cameras don’t focus on puddles the storm left behind. As the ambassador and his wife Lauren Ware Fertitta and their 5-year-old daughter, Elle, wrap up with us in the kitchen, guests have started to arrive: American military officers, in uniform, from nearby bases; regional government officials and Italian business leaders, in smart casual and linen, hoping for American investment. Once onboard, the guests munch on deviled eggs and mozzarella balls and snap selfies in front of one of the yacht’s two swimming pools before lining up for an official photo with the ambassador. ‘Between envy and admiration’ Everything is intentional on Fertitta’s yacht, starting on the mantel visitors see first with a silver-framed photo of him in a shoulder-to-shoulder-to-shoulder bipartisan embrace with former US presidents Bill Clinton and George Bush, Sr. Copies of his latest book “Shut up and Listen” are strategically placed, but there aren’t very many American flags inside the yacht, save the red, white and blue bunting on the outer railings. Fertitta says he is politically conservative. Records show he has made donations to former US president Joe Biden, but not to the extent he has supported candidates from his fellow Texan Bush family, and more recently Trump, who he has known for the better part of 25 years. He has hosted “most” of the US presidents since Clinton at his homes, but political affiliations remain in the eye of the beholder. “If you go back and you look at Bill Clinton back then, he would have been a conservative,” he says. “You know politics have probably gone too far in each direction, but I’m happy with what our president has done and I think he’s made everybody in Europe realize how important NATO is.” Fertitta is proud of slaloming the line “between envy and admiration,” as he puts it, when he invites people to mingle with him shipboard at every port of call: “I’m not doing this to show off. I’m doing this because it works for American and Italian relationships and it works for Ambassador Fertitta’s relationships with all the people in these little towns.” The tour, which will wrap up before Labor Day, has been cheered and jeered as it has docked in more than a dozen Italian port towns. In Cefalu, Sicily, he walked the same streets as his Italian ancestors and was given archival documents from the city relating to his family. In Venice, he received the same “F**k wealth/No kings” greeting that Jeff Bezos got when he married Lauren Sanchez there last summer. The ambassador says he is unfazed by the criticism. “It doesn’t bother me in the least because protesting doesn’t bother me,” he tells us from one of the large white leather sofas on the yacht’s main deck. “People would say, ‘Are you going to cancel?’ Absolutely not. I would even go up and talk to the protesters. I don’t mind hearing what they have to say.” Fertitta is the founder of the holding company Landry’s, which owns hundreds of restaurants, hotels and casinos across the United States. On the high end of the chains in its portfolio, the conglomerate owns Morton’s The Steakhouse, Mastro’s and The Palm. But Fertitta also has his thumbprint on casual and family dining spots like the Rainforest Cafe franchise and Bubba Gump Shrimp Company. He owns the Golden Nugget Hotels and Casinos and the NBA’s Houston Rockets NBA franchise and was the host of a reality TV program called Billion Dollar Buyer. He believes his business acumen and successful track record make him an asset to President Trump’s diplomatic mission: “I am a different ambassador, and they love that I have the ability to pick up the phone, politically or business-wise or entertainment-wise, and get somebody on the phone.” Fertitta is funding the summer excursion himself — save for the tight security, provided by the Italian government for an undisclosed amount, which has raised eyebrows and made headlines wherever he goes. Fertitta says protecting the American ambassador helps the Italian security personnel stay active. “Remember, those boats are out there doing something and those people are out there doing something, and it’s a great exercise for them,” he says. “Because there’s a lot more important people than me that they protect at times, so they’re getting good practice. But it’s been nothing crazy or unusual. …That’s the opposition’s job, to find something wrong with this.” In many ways, Boardwalk is Fertitta’s unofficial embassy, much in the way the Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida is President Trump’s unofficial White House. The stated purpose of this diplomacy jaunt is to strengthen the bonds between the Italian and American people, a task that was challenged recently during President Trump’s spat with Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni, a former Trump favorite who was the only European leader who attended his second-term inauguration. Fertitta brushes off the scuffle between his president and Meloni. Trump accused her of “begging for a selfie” last June during the G7 meeting in France and suggested he needed a restraining order against her. “The president has a great sense of humor, okay?” Fertitta says. “And he was using his sense of humor about that.” Fertitta agrees with President Trump on all the things an American ambassador is expected to, including major foreign policy issues like the war in Iran and the administration’s hardline immigration stance, which is echoed in Italy’s own internal policies, and he says he hopes he can do some work on the tariff battle. He considers himself among a stable of unconventional ambassadors appointed in Trump’s second term, along with Callista Gingrich in Switzerland and Charles Kushner in France. “Italy loves having an ambassador that has a little cachet and can get things done, and who is different and who has Italian heritage,” he says. The best fried zucchini flowers Fertitta went through five smaller yachts before commissioning this one in 2022, for delivery this spring, from the century-and-a-half-old Lürssen shipbuilding company. Inside, it has an eclectic, modern decor that Fertitta takes credit for choosing himself, guided by the interior designer Amy Halffman who died of cancer last year at the age of 52. The Fertitta family’s most valuable art is back in Rome at the ambassador’s residence, which they’ve spent time and their own money renovating since Fertitta took up his ambassadorship in May 2025, and in their family homes in Texas. But the ship has plenty of Murano glass including their new favorite: a thick rope chain sculpture called “Not all chains deter” by Edgardo Osorio, which they picked up this summer in Venice. One of the few art pieces that they did bring from their previous yacht to this one is a large red Craig Alan painting of Marilyn Monroe, the features composed of his signature groups of little human figures. There’s also an original bronze by Estella Fransbergen in the hallway leading up to the piano room. Italian tenor Andrea Bocelli, a fellow yachtsman who became friends with Fertitta after they met on the water last year, played the Boardwalk’s white grand piano when he stopped by a few nights earlier. “I’ve had lots of people play piano on my boats before, and at my homes, but he does something to make it sound better than everybody else,” Fertitta says, pulling up a video of the performance on his phone to prove his point. “You just watch the way his hands dance. Okay, it’s crazy. It’s beautiful and his voice sounds so great right now. He’s an unbelievable talent. It’s great to have him as a friend.” The Boardwalk’s two swimming pools, two helipads, putting green, spa with his- and-hers massage tables, and cinema exude a new money aesthetic. The yacht has gaudy chandeliers, shiny fittings, a glass elevator and more marble and mosaic tiles than most Italian villas. But for all the sheen, there are plenty of signs of a family home: a KitchenAid mixer and a baby bottle sterilizer, for the grandkids, sit on the kitchen workbench. The fridge, he lets us see, is full of leftovers. What was originally designed as the yacht’s library was repurposed as Elle’s playroom. Lauren Ware Fertitta says she personally designed the play area to incorporate more storage, which she says is somehow unbelievably lacking on the huge vessel. “You never have enough storage to hide things away,” she tells us. On the tour, Fertitta is excited to take our crew down to the bowels of the ship, guiding us through the polished engine rooms on full display behind glass, and on to the big kid toy room full of tenders, jet skis and what looks like a stealth submarine they call “the limo” to ferry guests from the yacht to shore. Despite pleas from his assistants to send out a warning of our arrival, Fertitta is intent on popping in on the crew unawares. One of his Italian helicopter pilots is caught jogging on a treadmill in a crew gym Fertitta describes as “way better than ours upstairs.” Then he slides the door open on the commercial kitchen where his chef, Tammy Steiger, who has cooked for him on this and his other yachts for ten years, is putting the finishing touches on the canapés for the impending reception many decks above. Fertitta gushes over what he described as the “best stuffed zucchini flowers he’s ever tasted” before opening the fridges to show us the bounty of food on board. Steiger, who has been with him far longer than he’s been a diplomat, brushes it off, seemingly amused. His security detail trailing us up and down the boat look increasingly unamused. Fertitta says despite his wide-ranging business success, the US ambassador to Italy has had his eye on the job for a long time, ever since learning more about his own Italian roots. His relationship with President Trump goes back to 1999, when Fertitta developed a Rainforest Café in the Trump Plaza Hotel and Casino. But he says it wasn’t a given that this was the administration that would finally provide his long-desired ambassadorship. “Being ambassador takes a lot of things to fall right,” he says. “You’ve got to choose the right candidate. You’ve got to stick with them. They’ve got to get elected then in the general election and then you have to have enough juice to get the country you want and for him to think you’re going to do a great job there. You have to catch lightning in a bottle to get a great position like this. I would have to say that even though I dream big, I hit the jackpot.”

articles.title: Sophie Cunningham’s Indiana Fever contract explained amid ‘release’ rumours circulating online

articles.body:
Sophie Cunningham has become one of the most high-profile names in the WNBA since her comments about protecting young girls from competing against biological males emerged last month.

Some people have thrown their support behind the Indiana Fever star, including using her face and image during rallies at WNBA games.

But there are others who have spoken out against Cunningham as the debate around transgender athletes competing in the league continues.

For example, some WNBA fans blamed Sophie for the Enes Kanter and Natasha Cloud incident at a recent Fever game.

But regardless of what you think about Cunningham's views, she has gained a lot of attention in the last month or so, and with the newfound notoriety has come more rumours.

In recent days, a number of accounts on X/Twitter have aggregated that she is going to be 'released' by the Fever after the 2026 season is over, citing 'WNBA sources' when doing so.

Sophie Cunningham set to become unrestricted free agent after one-year Fever deal

Amid talk of a release, we have taken a look at Sophie's current contract situation.

Back in April 2026, the Fever agreed a one-year deal with Sophie, which Spotrac says is worth $665,000.

Then, in 2027, when Cunningham's contract with her current team is up, she is listed as a 'UFA' (unrestricted free agent) on their site.

So, at present, Sophie is on course to leave the Fever after this year and become a free agent.

When she becomes an unrestricted free agent, as per the WNBA, 'A UFA is a player who can negotiate with any team during the free agency period without hindrance.'

Whether or not the Fever decide to negotiate a new deal with Cunningham beyond this year remains to be seen, of course, while a number of fans on social media have responded to suggestions she is going to be released.

One stated: "You can't be released when you're a free agent she's only on a one-year contract so she'll be a free agent. Now, whether they choose to re-sign her or not, that's different."

Another commented: "She's a free agent she can't be released by any team."

And a third echoed : "She is an UNRESTRICTED FREE AGENT at the end of the year. She has the rights to sign with whatever team she chooses to. 100% different than Sophie being released."
